claimed.text: The Times reported that Elizondo ran the programme from the Pentagon's fifth floor, resigned on 4 October in a letter to Defense Secretary Jim Mattis, and had joined To The Stars Academy with Puthoff and Mellon; it quoted Bigelow saying he had modified Las Vegas buildings to store recovered metal alloys.
Politico reported that Pentagon spokeswoman Dana White confirmed Elizondo directed the programme.
Elizondo says he ran AATIP out of OUSD(I) from about 2010 until he resigned, and wrote to Pentagon spokesperson Susan Gough in June 2020 that everyone involved knows he ran the program.

Mellon says he received the videos in the Pentagon parking lot from a Defense Department official and gave them to the Times; the Times separately said the Department of Defense was its on-the-record source for them. The official who handed them over has never been identified.

Michael Shellenberger's whistleblower source alleges that the Defense Department created the Immaculate Constellation programme in 2017 in response to the Times story; the claim is attributed, not documented.
Reid later said $22 million was not enough and that failing to study the subject would be malpractice.

When the same two reporters brought Grusch's crash-retrieval claims to The Debrief in June 2023, after, by contemporaneous reporting, national outlets had declined the story, they carried on-record corroboration from Karl Nell and from Mellon, who said well-placed current and former officials had shared detailed information with him.

contested.text: Since June 2019 the Department has said Elizondo had no assigned responsibilities for AATIP, that DIA administered it and that he interacted with it but did not lead it.

AARO's Historical Record Report Volume I says AATIP was never an official DoD program and that the name was later used by an informal community of interest, and that none of the programmes interviewees mentioned are reverse-engineering programmes. On the board's reading, the never-official line depends on which of the names DIA used interchangeably is treated as canonical.
The records do not agree on the programme's name: one 2009 DoD packet carries AAWSAP as the official title, AAITP as Reid's usage and AATIP as the unclassified nickname.
The records date Reid's letter to Lynn differently, one to 24 June 2009 and another to 24 July 2009.
The Times reported the resignation as a 4 October letter to Mattis, while the letter released under FOIA is dated 3 October 2017 with the resignation effective 4 October.
The videos were cleared for research and sharing, not for publication, and To The Stars Academy's framing of them as officially cleared was contested by the Navy in September 2019.
Former AARO director Sean Kirkpatrick has attributed the modern crash-retrieval narrative to AATIP and Robert Bigelow's circle.

record.text: The Times identified Reid as the senator who initiated and funded the programme, and quoted him saying he was not embarrassed or ashamed or sorry he got it going, and calling the appropriation black money.

On the Department's own account, given by spokesman Thomas Crosson, the programme existed, about $22 million was appropriated from late 2008 through 2011, most of it went to Bigelow Aerospace, and it was terminated in 2012.

DIA records Reid and Senator Daniel Inouye as sponsors of a $10 million add in the FY2008 supplemental appropriation to investigate foreign advanced aerospace weapon threats out to 40 years, followed by a $12 million add in FY2010.

In 2009 Reid wrote to Deputy Secretary of Defense William Lynn asking that the programme, which he called the AAITP, be placed under restricted special access protection with a bigoted access list; DIA scheduled a November 2009 briefing to tell him the deliverables did not meet the criteria for a special access programme.

Three weeks after the story, on 9 January 2018, DIA told the Senate Armed Services Committee that the purpose of AATIP was to investigate foreign advanced aerospace weapon threats out to the next 40 years, and enclosed a list of 38 products.

Elizondo submitted a DD Form 1910 on 9 August 2017 to clear the GoFast, Gimbal and FLIR video files, approved on 24 August 2017, with the stated purpose of research, analysis and information sharing, not publication. His resignation as Director, National Programs Special Management Staff, in OUSD(I) took effect on 4 October 2017.

On 10 September 2019 the Navy designated the objects in the videos as unidentified aerial phenomena, and on 27 April 2020 the Department authorised release of the three videos, saying the phenomena in them remain characterized as unidentified.

To The Stars Academy's SEC filings list Tom DeLonge, Jim Semivan and Harold Puthoff as directors, Elizondo and Steve Justice as significant employees, and Mellon on the advisory board as a former Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defense for Intelligence.

summary.text: The story named Elizondo as the official who ran the programme, quoted his resignation letter and reported his move to To The Stars Academy; the Pentagon's spokesman confirmed that the programme existed and had been shut down in 2012.

The programme behind the name is DIA's AAWSAP contract, funded by $22 million in appropriations that Reid sponsored; three weeks after the story DIA wrote to the Senate Armed Services Committee about it.

Elizondo had requested internal clearance of the videos in August 2017 on a form stating they were not for publication, and it was approved; Christopher Mellon says he received them from a Defense Department official and passed them to the paper; the Navy later designated them unidentified and the Department released them outright in April 2020.

On the board's reading the story added no new physical evidence but changed the subject's institutional standing, and later official acts follow it in sequence. Kean and Blumenthal went on to report David Grusch's claims in 2023, at The Debrief rather than the Times.

title: The December 2017 New York Times story
